text: 3 Bayesian Sheaf Neural Networks
In this section, we introduce a Bayesian framework for Sheaf Neural Networks, extending the deterministic architecture by incorporating uncertainty in the learned sheaf structure.
3.1 Problem Statement

Consider a semi-supervised node classification problem, in which we have a graph dataset G = ( V , E ) G=(V,E) together with a node feature matrix X X , a collection of observed node labels, y y , and a collection of unobserved node labels, y ∗ y^{*} , all of which are random samples. We model the conditional probability p θ ​ ( y | X ) p_{\theta}(y|X) using a sheaf neural network whose layers are given by Eq.( 3 ), with network parameters θ \theta , adjacency matrix A A , and a cellular sheaf ℱ \mathcal{F} .

Rather than taking the learned cellular sheaf ℱ \mathcal{F} to be a deterministic function of X X , we regard ℱ \mathcal{F} as a latent random variable of our model. See Figure 1 for a depiction of the probability graphical model. Note that the posterior distribution p θ ​ ( ℱ | X , y ) p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}|X,y) will be intractable due to the fact that the labels y y are modeled as the output of a neural network.

To approximate posterior inference of ℱ \mathcal{F} given the feature matrix X X , the observed node labels y y , and model parameters θ \theta , we assume that the intractable posterior distribution p θ ​ ( ℱ | X , y ) p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}|X,y) belongs to a predetermined family of variational distributions q ϕ ​ ( ℱ | X , y ) q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y) parameterized by weights ϕ \phi as discussed in Section 2.4 . In our framework, we choose priors for ℱ \mathcal{F} that reflect plausible variability in sheaf structures while preserving the tractability of inference.

3.2 Variational Sheaf Learner

We make the simplifying assumption that the variational distribution q ϕ ​ ( ℱ | X , y ) q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y) from the previous section factors as the product ∏ u ​ ⊴ ​ e q ϕ ​ ( ℱ u ​ ⊴ ​ e | X , y ) \prod_{u\trianglelefteq e}q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}|X,y) over all incident node-edge pairs u ​ ⊴ ​ e u\trianglelefteq e . While this assumption somewhat restricts the family of variational distributions, it makes computing the KL divergence term in the ELBO tractable. For further details, see Appendix Appendix C: KL Divergence Calculations .

For each incident node-edge pair u ​ ⊴ ​ e u\trianglelefteq e , if u ′ ​ ⊴ ​ e u^{\prime}\trianglelefteq e denotes the other node incident with e e , a multi-layer perceptron with learned weights ϕ \phi , denoted MLP ϕ \MLP_{\phi} , maps the concatenated vector [ x u | | x u ′ ] [x_{u}||x_{u^{\prime}}] to distributional parameters μ u ​ ⊴ ​ e \mu_{u\trianglelefteq e} and σ u ​ ⊴ ​ e \sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e} :

Case 3: Special Orthogonal. The class of sheaves with special orthogonal restriction maps is of particular interest for sheaf neural networks, including our Bayesian sheaf neural networks, due to both theoretical and practical properties. From a theoretical point of view, certain results concerning the kernel of Δ ℱ \Delta_{\mathcal{F}} can be proven for sheaves using rotations as restriction maps [ 10 , Section 3.1] . Regarding the more practical aspects, rotations offer a nice middle-ground between diagonal and general linear maps in terms of balancing the number of parameters with the expressivity of the resulting sheaf. Moreover, when using rotations, the blocks along the diagonal of the sheaf Laplacian L ℱ L_{\mathcal{F}} are scalar multiples of the identity matrix. This makes computing the normalized sheaf Laplacian Δ ℱ \Delta_{\mathcal{F}} easier.

These properties motivate our focus on S ​ O ​ ( d ) SO(d) sheaves. To further support their utility, we extend previous theoretical results on their separation power as defined in Section 2.2 . In particular, we prove that for any number of classes C ∈ ℕ C\in\mathbb{N} , we may find d d large enough such that ℋ s ​ o d \mathcal{H}_{so}^{d} has linear separation power over 𝒢 C \mathcal{G}_{C} . In the following proposition, ⌊ ⋅ ⌋ \lfloor\cdot\rfloor denotes the floor function.
Proposition 1 .

For any d ≥ 1 d\geq 1 , if 𝒢 \mathcal{G} denotes the class of connected graphs with C ≤ 7 ​ ⌊ d 4 ⌋ C\leq 7\lfloor\tfrac{d}{4}\rfloor classes, then ℋ s ​ o d \mathcal{H}_{so}^{d} has linear separation power over 𝒢 \mathcal{G} .
For a proof see Appendix Appendix A: Proof of Proposition .

We now turn to the practical challenge of incorporating these S ​ O ​ ( d ) SO(d) maps into the variational model. Typical probability distributions on S ​ O ​ ( d ) SO(d) , such as the matrix Langevin distribution, are not easily reparameterizable. This makes incorporating such distributions into neural networks that are trained via back-propagation difficult. On the other hand, while reparameterizable distributions on S ​ O ​ ( d ) SO(d) have been constructed in [ 27 ] using the exponential map, the density functions of such distributions can be difficult to compute exactly, which obstructs one from computing, or even efficiently estimating, the KL divergence term in Eq.( 18 ).

In Section 3.3 , we introduce Cayley distributions, a family of reparameterizable distributions 𝒞 d ​ ( M , κ ) \mathcal{C}_{d}(M,\kappa) on S ​ O ​ ( d ) SO(d) with closed form expressions for their probability density functions. We use 𝒞 d ​ ( M , κ ) \mathcal{C}_{d}(M,\kappa) as the variational distributions for sheaves with special orthogonal restriction maps. Hence when ℱ u ​ ⊴ ​ e ∈ S ​ O ​ ( d ) \mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}\in SO(d) , the distributional parameters are a mean rotation μ u ​ ⊴ ​ e ∈ S ​ O ​ ( d ) \mu_{u\trianglelefteq e}\in SO(d) and scalar concentration parameter σ u ​ ⊴ ​ e ∈ [ 0 , 1 ) \sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e}\in[0,1) , and we have Q ⁡ ( μ u ​ ⊴ ​ e , σ u ​ ⊴ ​ e ) = 𝒞 d ​ ( μ u ​ ⊴ ​ e , σ u ​ ⊴ ​ e ) Q(\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e},\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e})=\mathcal{C}_{d}(\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e},\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e}) . The reparameterization of the Cayley distributions is described in Remark 7 . We use a prior distribution p θ ​ ( ℱ ) = ∏ u ​ ⊴ ​ e p θ ​ ( ℱ u ​ ⊴ ​ e ) p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F})=\prod_{u\trianglelefteq e}p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}) where each p θ ​ ( ℱ u ​ ⊴ ​ e ) p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}) is a uniform distribution on S ​ O ​ ( d ) SO(d) .

3.4 Bayesian Sheaf Neural Network Architecture

We present the Bayesian sheaf neural network architecture, which is also summarized in Figure 2 and Algorithm 1 . The variational sheaf learning mechanism maps the input node features to the sheaf distributional parameters as described in Section 3.2 , For completeness, we briefly review the mechanism here as well.

A linear layer first resizes the input node features to dimension k k . Specifically, we use k = d ​ f k=df where d d and f f are the stalk dimensions and number of feature channels respectively. For each edge e = ( u , u ′ ) ∈ E e=(u,u^{\prime})\in E , we consider the two incident node-edge pairs u ​ ⊴ ​ e u\trianglelefteq e and u ′ ​ ⊴ ​ e u^{\prime}\trianglelefteq e . For each pair, we construct a feature vector by concatenating the features of the node with those of the node at the other end of the edge. Hence, a node feature matrix of size n × k n\times k is transformed by this concatenation operation into a matrix of size 2 ​ e × 2 ​ k 2e\times 2k , where n n denotes the number of nodes, and e e denotes the number of edges in the graph.

Lastly, an MLP maps these features indexed by the incident node-edge pairs u ​ ⊴ ​ e u\trianglelefteq e to distributional parameters μ u ​ ⊴ ​ e \mu_{u\trianglelefteq e} and σ u ​ ⊴ ​ e \sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e} as described by Eq.( 21 ), which define the distribution over the cellular sheaves. From this distribution, a collection of independent and identically distributed sheaves ℱ 1 , ℱ 2 , … , ℱ L \mathcal{F}_{1},\mathcal{F}_{2},\dots,\mathcal{F}_{L} are sampled: one for each layer of the network.

Separately, a multi-layer perceptron maps the input node features X ∈ ℝ n × m X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m} to features of dimension X ′ ∈ ℝ n × d ​ f X^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times df} where d d is the stalk dimension and f f is the number of hidden channels. The features X ′ X^{\prime} are reshaped to size n ​ d × f nd\times f .

Sheaf layers described by Eq.( 3 ) update the transformed features X ′ X^{\prime} using the sampled sheaves ℱ 1 , ℱ 2 , … , ℱ L \mathcal{F}_{1},\mathcal{F}_{2},\dots,\mathcal{F}_{L} . Finally, a linear layer maps the output of the final sheaf layer to a vector of class probabilities.

During training, a one-sample Monte Carlo estimate of Eq.( 19 ) or Eq.( 20 ) is computed, and the loss is back-propagated to update the network weights. During testing, multiple sheaf samples are drawn from the learned posterior, and ensembling is performed over the corresponding forward passes to obtain point estimates for the unobserved node labels y ∗ y^{*} .
